note: Implementations of SHRDLU: copies and states of Winograd’s program, ports, translations, reimplementations and SHRDLU-like programs, with declared descent. Parents name an I-code or a variorum version (v:jan71, v:c1, v:mit, v:stanford, v:ejs). Files not yet cleared stay in the paratext archive, named in heldAt.

families.name: Winograd’s SHRDLU
families.note: The program’s own states and their copies: the MIT ITS directories, the 1997 Stanford distribution and its mirrors, Svensson’s and the course copies, Swenson’s 2024 restoration and Pereira’s reconstruction of the thesis-era image. The variorum versions (v:jan71, v:c1, v:mit, v:stanford, v:ejs) are its roots.

families.name: The UMR Common Lisp port
families.note: The University of Missouri-Rolla student project’s port of the distribution from MacLisp to Common Lisp (1999-2000), its console and Java 3D versions, and the repositories that carry them on.

families.name: Translations of the source
families.note: Whole-program translations of the distribution into another language.

families.name: Micro-Planner
families.note: The planner SHRDLU runs on (Sussman, Winograd and Charniak), with its own ports.

families.name: Reimplementations
families.note: Programs written anew from published descriptions of SHRDLU, aiming to do what it did.

families.name: SHRDLU-like programs and homages
families.note: Blocks-world and natural-language programs modelled on SHRDLU or named after it, from the 1970s to now, including magazine and textbook programs. Their descent is from the idea, not the code.

features.label: Systemic grammar
features.note: A parser for Halliday-style systemic grammar written in PROGRAMMAR, as in Winograd’s program.

features.label: Micro-Planner
features.note: Deduction and action by Micro-Planner theorems (THGOAL, THASSERT, THCONSE).

features.label: Blocks display
features.note: The blocks world drawn on a screen (Type 340, Java 3D, a browser).

features.label: Runs the 1970 dialogue
features.note: Carries out the published demonstration dialogue (Understanding Natural Language, section 1.3), or most of it.

features.label: Why-questions
features.note: Answers questions about its own past actions from an event history (“Why did you pick it up?”).

items.title: shrdlu-1971-restaurado: SHRDLU da época da tese (1970–71): decodificado e rodando de novo
items.creator: Pereira, Samuel Russel
items.rights: MIT License for the new work (scripts, analyses, adjustments); redistributed historical files "mantém os direitos de origem" (NOTICE.md), as the README states.
items.extent: Repository of 251 files: 129 are copies of PDP-10/its and its-vault files (matched by git blob hash against the held sets and beat A downloads); the rest are decoding scripts, diffs, thesis page crops, transcripts
items.description: A reconstruction published the day before this sweep. Pereira (working with Claude) identifies the its-vault MOBY DUMP and Z files (A-01) as the thesis-era SHRDLU, decodes the image (234 of 238 comparable interpreted definitions identical to the Z files; Micro-Planner database = the 73 assertions of AI-TR-235 Appendix F) and runs it on the KA10 emulator: "36 das 46 respostas do diálogo da tese palavra por palavra" with 17 documented code interventions and 4 variables, 20 with none. It also reports, in 06_verificacoes/smspec_corrupcao_stanford.diff, that the smspec in Winograd's 1997 Stanford distribution has 25 bit-damaged lines (SMONE3, SMPOSS/SMPOSS2, SMRELATE) that the ITS copy lacks; beat A confirmed this by diffing the held original/code/smspec against its/as-found/smspec.94. Its claims about tapes, the pidp-10 group and Swenson's conversation with Winograd are Pereira's and are secondary here.

parents.evidence: The reconstruction decodes the its-vault MOBY DUMP and Z files (P-DVNCN).

It is a small blocks-world conversation program: CONVERSE prints HELLO, reads a sentence, parses it against phrase-structure rules (P-RULES, PARSE ... <S>), interprets it against a FACTS list of BOX, BALL, BLOCK, TABLE and FLOOR, and resolves IT ("ASSUMING BY 'IT' YOU MEAN"); it ends "MINI-LINGUISTIC SYSTEM READY". It is a 1970s teaching derivative of SHRDLU from CMU, the site where Card ported the program in 1972; who the Stanford student was and when the edit was made are not stated.
